title: Holy Thursday
hook: the washing of feet, the new commandment, and the watch at the altar of repose

segments.voice: Yesterday, the holy oils, blessed at the Chrism Mass and sent to every parish. Your line was oil for the whole year.

In English the day is sometimes called Maundy Thursday, an odd word that hides its meaning. In Britain the monarch gives out special coins that day. In parish churches something stranger happens: after the homily, the priest takes off his outer vestment, ties a towel around his waist, kneels on the floor, and washes the feet of people chosen from the congregation. The odd English word and the odd ritual come from the same Latin word.
screen: `MAUNDY THURSDAY.` → `A TOWEL AROUND THE WAIST.` → `ONE LATIN WORD.`

segments.voice: Holy Thursday evening begins the Triduum, the three great days. The Mass of the Lord's Supper remembers the night Jesus gave his disciples the Eucharist, and the gospel is John 13. During supper, Jesus gets up, lays aside his garments, takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and washes his disciples' feet, a job usually left to servants. Peter protests: you will never wash my feet. Jesus says, if I don't wash you, you have no part with me. Then he sits back down and explains: if I, your Lord and master, have washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's. And a little later, the command: "A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another, as I have loved you." In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and from mandatum comes maundy. So the rite of foot washing is called the Mandatum. The Gloria is sung tonight with the bells ringing, and then the bells fall silent until the Easter Vigil. After communion, the remaining consecrated hosts are carried in procession to a side altar, the altar of repose, decked with flowers and candles. The main altar is stripped bare. And people stay. They keep watch, often until midnight, remembering Gethsemane, where Jesus asked his friends to stay awake while he prayed in anguish, and found them sleeping. In the Douay-Rheims: "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" On this night, some Catholics walk from church to church, visiting several altars of repose, keeping company with him in each.
screen: `THE TRIDUUM BEGINS.` · `A TOWEL AND A BASIN.` · `MANDATUM: THE NEW COMMANDMENT.` · `THE WATCH AT THE ALTAR OF REPOSE.` · then, large: `LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.`

segments.voice: On this night people keep watch at the altar of repose, and an hour is the old measure; for now, sit wherever you are and keep company. Picture the garden, olive trees, the dark, friends asleep, one man praying, and stay awake with him. If you pray, simply stay, no words needed; if you don't, keep watch for someone you know who is suffering tonight.
Mandatum. Latin for commandment: the new commandment to love one another, the foot washing named for it, and the root of maundy. Today's word.
Your line: love one another. The towel and the basin show what that looks like. That's day six hundred sixty.

howItsDone: At the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest may wash the feet of members of the congregation, the Eucharist is carried to an altar of repose, the main altar is stripped, and the faithful keep watch, often until midnight.

chat.says: Why is it called Maundy Thursday? What does maundy even mean?
options: It comes from mandatum, Latin for commandment: love one another, as I have loved you.
It's an old English word for washing, taken from the foot washing that night.
It's an old word for mourning, because this is the day the Passion begins.
